claim: AAV expressing GCaMP6s was stereotaxically injected into the piriform cortex of adult (6- to 10-week-old) mice.
source: We stereotaxically injected adeno-associated virus (AAV) expressing the calcium indicator GCaMP6s (Chen et al., 2013) into the piriform cortex of adult (6- to 10-week-old) mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental procedure performed.

claim: Ten days after AAV-GCaMP6s infection, the piriform cortex was surgically exposed for two-photon imaging under ketamine/xylazine anesthesia.
source: Ten days after infection, we surgically exposed the piriform cortex for two-photon imaging under ketamine/xylazine anesthesia.
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline and conditions.

claim: Viral expression of GCaMP6s resulted in dense labeling of layer II piriform neurons.
source: Viral expression of GCaMP6s resulted in dense labeling of layer II piriform neurons (Figure 1a and b, and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: An automated cell segmentation algorithm based on calcium signal similarities was developed to monitor calcium signals in large and densely packed neural ensembles.
source: To monitor calcium signals in such large and densely packed neural ensembles, we developed an automated cell segmentation algorithm based on calcium signal similarities (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Materials and methods).
evidence: The development of the algorithm is described and illustrated in the supplementary figure.

claim: The automated cell segmentation algorithm operates on the entire data set and efficiently identifies individual neurons by iteratively clustering neighboring pixels with high-signal covariance.
source: This algorithm operates on the entire data set obtained from individual imaging sites and efficiently identifies individual neurons by iteratively clustering neighboring pixels with high-signal covariance.
evidence: This describes the operational principle of the algorithm.

claim: 100–400 neurons (mean ± SD: 242 ± 105) could be simultaneously monitored per imaging site.
source: Under these conditions, we could simultaneously monitor the activity of 100–400 (mean ± SD: 242 ± 105) neurons per imaging site.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiments.

claim: Two-second odor pulses of monomolecular odorants at 1:10,000 dilution elicited relatively sparse but partially overlapping activity of piriform neurons.
source: Two-second odor pulses of these stimuli (1:10,000 dilution in mineral oil, 0.01% vol./vol.) elicited relatively sparse but partially overlapping activity of piriform neurons, consistent with one previously published report (Stettler and Axel, 2009) (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: This observation is supported by the imaging data and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Individual piriform neurons responded selectively with an increase or decrease in fluorescence.
source: We observed that individual neurons responded selectively with an increase or decrease in fluorescence.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the calcium imaging data.

claim: Across six imaging sites in three mice (total number of neurons = 1706), 20% (±8.4%) of the neurons responded with an increase in fluorescence, and 11% (±5.7%) of the neurons responded with a decrease in fluorescence.
source: Across six imaging sites in three mice (total number of neurons = 1706), 20% (±8.4%) of the neurons responded with an increase in fluorescence, and 11% (±5.7%) of the neurons responded with a decrease in fluorescence (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the response data.

claim: Most neurons responding with an increase in fluorescence exhibited narrow stimulus tuning, with the exception of a small subpopulation of neurons (8.5 ± 5.4%) that responded to 12 or all 13 odorants of the test panel.
source: Most neurons responding with an increase in fluorescence exhibited narrow stimulus tuning, with the exception of a small subpopulation of neurons (8.5 ± 5.4%) that responded to 12 or all 13 odorants of the test panel.
evidence: This describes the tuning properties of the responding neurons.

claim: Neurons responding with a decrease in fluorescence exhibited similarly selective odor tuning, but only a minimal number of broadly tuned neurons could be observed.
source: Neurons responding with a decrease in fluorescence exhibited similarly selective odor tuning, but only a minimal number of broadly tuned neurons could be observed (Figure 1g).
evidence: This describes the tuning properties of suppressed neurons.

claim: Many piriform neurons displayed high trial-to-trial variability in response to the repeated delivery of the same odorant.
source: Strikingly, many neurons displayed high trial-to-trial variability in response to the repeated delivery of the same odorant (Figure 1e).
evidence: This observation is supported by the reliability data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Repeated exposure to the same odorant triggered highly correlated population response patterns (intra-odorant cross-trial correlation coefficients: 0.67 ± 0.07).
source: As indicated by the square boxes along the diagonal (4 × 4 trials), repeated exposure to the same odorant triggered highly correlated population response patterns (intra-odorant cross-trial correlation coefficients, neurons pooled across six imaging sites: 0.67 ± 0.07 (across odorants)).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of response similarity across trials.

claim: Patterns elicited by different odorants were fairly similar (mean inter-odorant correlation coefficient: 0.44 ± 0.08).
source: However, this cross-correlation analysis also revealed that patterns elicited by different odorants were fairly similar (mean inter-odorant correlation coefficient: 0.44 ± 0.08).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of response similarity between different odorants.

claim: Despite trial-to-trial variability and considerable overlap in response patterns to different odorants, a linear classifier could correctly identify all 13 stimuli in the odorant test panel.
source: Despite both trial-to-trial variability and considerable overlap in response patterns to different odorants, the classifier could correctly identify all 13 stimuli in our odorant test panel (Figure 2d).
evidence: This demonstrates that odor identity information is present in the population response patterns.

claim: Classification accuracy reached 94% when pooling all six imaging sites.
source: Classification accuracy reached 94% when pooling all six imaging sites (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of decoding performance.

claim: For individual imaging sites, the average classification accuracy was 71% (±5.8%).
source: For individual imaging sites, the average classification accuracy was 71% (±5.8%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of decoding performance at individual sites.

claim: Correct classification slowly rises after odor onset to reach high accuracy within 0.5 s.
source: Correct classification slowly rises after odor onset to reach high accuracy within 0.5 s.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of classification accuracy.

claim: The relatively slow rise in classification accuracy can largely be explained by the slow rise time of the calcium indicator GCAMP6s.
source: This relatively slow rise can largely be explained by the slow rise time of the calcium indicator GCAMP6s (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of GCaMP6s.

claim: Classification accuracy remained significantly above chance level for several seconds after odor delivery, despite a marked decline in odor-evoked fluorescence.
source: Interestingly, classification accuracy remained significantly above chance level for several seconds after odor delivery, despite a marked decline in odor-evoked fluorescence (Figure 2e).
evidence: This observation suggests persistent odor-specific network configurations.

claim: This finding is consistent with the observation that odor-specific network configurations persist for extended periods of time in the olfactory bulb.
source: This finding is consistent with the observation that odor-specific network configurations persist for extended periods of time in the olfactory bulb (Bathellier et al., 2008; Friedrich and Laurent, 2001).
evidence: This relates the current finding to prior observations in the olfactory bulb.

claim: A classifier trained on response patterns 1 s after odor onset accurately predicted odor identity during odor delivery, but classification accuracy readily declined after odor offset.
source: We observed that a classifier trained on response patterns 1 s after odor onset accurately predicted odor identity during odor delivery, but classification accuracy readily declined after odor offset.
evidence: This describes the temporal specificity of odor representations.

claim: A classifier based on response patterns at 0.27 and 3 s after odor onset yielded a lower classification accuracy; however, classification success was more stable over time.
source: In contrast, a classifier based on response patterns at 0.27 and 3 s after odor onset yielded a lower classification accuracy; however, classification success was more stable over time.
evidence: This describes the temporal stability of different odor representations.

claim: Early and late (post-odor offset) representations are based on weak activity configurations present during odor exposure but masked by another much stronger component, which quickly vanishes after the odor is withdrawn.
source: This suggests that early and late (post-odor offset) representations are based on weak activity configurations present during odor exposure but masked by another much stronger component, which quickly vanishes after the odor is withdrawn.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the classification results.

claim: Odor representations are dynamically rearranged after odor offset to maintain odor information for several seconds.
source: Thus, odor representations are dynamically rearranged after odor offset to maintain odor information for several seconds.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal dynamics of classification accuracy.

claim: Previous anatomical and functional experiments suggested that odor information was encoded in randomly distributed ensembles of piriform neurons.
source: Previous anatomical and functional experiments suggested that odor information was encoded in randomly distributed ensembles of piriform neurons (Ghosh et al., 2011; Illig and Haberly, 2003; Sosulski et al., 2011; Stettler and Axel, 2009).
evidence: This summarizes prior findings from the literature.

claim: No evidence for spatial clustering of odorant-selective piriform neurons was found in any of the six imaging sites (p values of 0.49, 0.81, 0.09, 0.21, 0.91, 0.79).
source: Using this measure, we found no evidence for spatial clustering in any of the six imaging sites (p values of 0.49, 0.81, 0.09, 0.21, 0.91, 0.79).
evidence: This is based on nearest neighbor index analysis.

claim: Information about odor identity is homogeneously distributed across individual imaging sites.
source: These observations suggest that information about odor identity is homogeneously distributed across individual imaging sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial analysis.

claim: Different clusters of the same size encoded odorant identity with similar accuracy, and no 'hotspots' of classification were observed.
source: We observed that different clusters of the same size encoded odorant identity with similar accuracy, and that no 'hotspots' of classification were observed.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of local neural ensembles.

claim: Classification accuracy was very similar for the six different imaging sites in three mice, which were up to 1 mm apart along the rostro-caudal axis of the piriform cortex.
source: Finally, we found that classification accuracy was very similar for the six different imaging sites in three mice, which were up to 1 mm apart along the rostro-caudal axis of the piriform cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and data not shown).
evidence: This demonstrates spatial consistency of odor coding.

claim: Odorants activate spatially distributed ensembles of piriform neurons with significant overlap and variability, and no apparent spatial organization.
source: Taken together, our data show that odorants activate spatially distributed ensembles of piriform neurons with significant overlap and variability, and no apparent spatial organization.
evidence: This is a summary of the spatial organization findings.

claim: The spatial patterns of odor-evoked piriform activity contain sufficient information to robustly decode stimulus identity.
source: Furthermore, the spatial patterns of odor-evoked piriform activity contain sufficient information to robustly decode stimulus identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the classification analysis.

claim: Perceived odor identity of monomolecular odorants typically remains stable across a large range of odor intensities.
source: Importantly, perceived odor identity of monomolecular odorants typically remains stable across a large range of odor intensities (Homma et al., 2009), providing an experimental opportunity to more directly address this question.
evidence: This is based on behavioral studies cited.

claim: The fraction of both activated and suppressed neurons increased moderately but statistically significantly with increasing concentrations.
source: We found that the fraction of both activated and suppressed neurons increased moderately but statistically significantly with increasing concentrations (Figure 4a and b, mixed effect ANOVA, significant effect of concentration on the fraction of activated neurons: F(2,96) = 52.49, p<0.01, and on the fraction of suppressed neurons: F(2,96) = 28.79, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the concentration-dependent responses.

claim: Population sparseness decreases with increasing concentrations.
source: Thus, population sparseness decreases with increasing concentrations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the observation that more neurons respond at higher concentrations.

claim: Diverse concentration-induced changes in cell selectivity were observed across the population, indicating that an increase in odorant concentration did not systematically broaden odor tuning.
source: We observed diverse concentration-induced changes in cell selectivity across the population, indicating that an increase in odorant concentration did not systematically broaden odor tuning (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of individual cell responses across concentrations.

claim: The distribution of lifetime sparseness of individual neurons was maintained across stimulus intensities (mean ± SD: 0.01%: 0.35 ± 0.23, 0.1%: 0.37 ± 0.24, 1%: 0.38 ± 0.24).
source: Indeed, when considered across the entire population, the distribution of lifetime sparseness of individual neurons was maintained across stimulus intensities (mean ± SD: 0.01%: 0.35 ± 0.23, 0.1%: 0.37 ± 0.24, 1%: 0.38 ± 0.24, Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of tuning stability across concentrations.

claim: Pair-wise trial correlations increased with concentration, indicating that trial-to-trial variability across the population decreases at higher concentrations (mean ± SD across odorants: 0.01%, 0.67 ± 0.03; 0.1%, 0.72 ± 0.06; 1%, 0.74 ± 0.05).
source: We first noted that pair-wise trial correlations increased with concentration, indicating that trial-to-trial variability across the population decreases at higher concentrations (mean ± SD across odorants: 0.01%, 0.67 ± 0.03; 0.1%, 0.72 ± 0.06; 1%, 0.74 ± 0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of response reliability across concentrations.

claim: Responses to a given odorant at a given concentration were significantly more correlated than responses to a given odorant at different concentrations (mixed-effect ANOVA, effect of concentration F2,96 = 51.39, p<0.01).
source: Furthermore, we found that responses to a given odorant at a given concentration were significantly more correlated than responses to a given odorant at different concentrations (mixed-effect ANOVA, effect of concentration F2,96 = 51.39, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis showing concentration-dependent decorrelation.

claim: The average correlation between response patterns elicited by the three odorants at low (0.01% vol./vol.) and intermediate (0.1% vol./vol.) concentrations was 0.53 (±0.12).
source: This concentration-dependent decorrelation was gradual: the average correlation between response patterns elicited by the three odorants at low (0.01% vol./vol.) and intermediate (0.1% vol./vol.) concentrations was 0.53 (±0.12), while the average correlation between response patterns at low and high (1% vol./vol.) odorant concentrations dropped to 0.36 (±0.12) (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of decorrelation across concentrations.

claim: The average correlation between response patterns at low and high (1% vol./vol.) odorant concentrations dropped to 0.36 (±0.12).
source: This concentration-dependent decorrelation was gradual: the average correlation between response patterns elicited by the three odorants at low (0.01% vol./vol.) and intermediate (0.1% vol./vol.) concentrations was 0.53 (±0.12), while the average correlation between response patterns at low and high (1% vol./vol.) odorant concentrations dropped to 0.36 (±0.12) (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of decorrelation across concentrations.

claim: The spatial patterns of piriform odor responses were not concentration-invariant.
source: Thus, the spatial patterns of piriform odor responses were not concentration-invariant.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the decorrelation analysis.

claim: Response patterns to a given odorant changed substantially as odor concentration increased and became as different over a 100-fold change in concentration as responses to a different odorant.
source: Instead, response patterns to a given odorant changed substantially as odor concentration increased and became as different over a 100-fold change in concentration as responses to a different odorant.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the correlation analysis.

claim: 37.2 ± 11.7% of cells were selectively responsive to odorant.
source: Consistent with our qualitative inspection of response profiles (Figure 5a and b), we found that 37.2 ± 11.7% of cells were selectively responsive to odorant, while 27.8 ± 10.6% of cells showed responses that were modulated by an interaction between odorant identity and concentration (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is based on ANOVA analysis of cell responses.

claim: 27.8 ± 10.6% of cells showed responses that were modulated by an interaction between odorant identity and concentration.
source: Consistent with our qualitative inspection of response profiles (Figure 5a and b), we found that 37.2 ± 11.7% of cells were selectively responsive to odorant, while 27.8 ± 10.6% of cells showed responses that were modulated by an interaction between odorant identity and concentration (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is based on ANOVA analysis of cell responses.

claim: Of the cells that were selectively modulated by odorant, 30.1% ± 11.6%, constituting 10.4 ± 4.5% of the total population of cells, exhibited concentration-invariant responses for all three odors.
source: Crucially, of the cells that were selectively modulated by odorant, 30.1% ± 11.6%, constituting 10.4 ± 4.5% of the total population of cells, exhibited concentration-invariant responses for all three odors, according to the analysis of variance (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is based on ANOVA analysis identifying concentration-invariant neurons.

claim: Although many neurons displayed mixed selectivity to the odorant identities and concentrations tested, a substantial fraction of concentration-invariant neurons can be identified within piriform neural ensembles.
source: Thus, although many neurons displayed mixed selectivity to the odorant identities and concentrations tested in our experiment, a substantial fraction of concentration-invariant neurons can be identified within piriform neural ensembles.
evidence: This is a summary of the ANOVA results.

claim: For a given odorant, responses of concentration-invariant neurons remained highly correlated across increasing concentrations (mean inter-concentration similarity ± SD across odorants, 0.01% to 0.1%: 0.60 ± 0.09; 0.01% to 1%: 0.57 ± 0.10).
source: We found that, for a given odorant, responses remained highly correlated across increasing concentrations (mean inter-concentration similarity ± SD across odorants, 0.01% to 0.1%: 0.60 ± 0.09; 0.01% to 1%: 0.57 ± 0.10, Figure 6d, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This validates the concentration-invariance of the selected neurons.

claim: Odorant representations of concentration-invariant neurons clustered irrespective of concentration, while odorant representations of generic neurons clustered by concentrations of the same odorants, but not systematically by odorant groups.
source: This analysis revealed that odorant representations of concentration-invariant neurons clustered irrespective of concentration, while odorant representations of generic neurons clustered by concentrations of the same odorants, but not systematically by odorant groups (Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of the response patterns.

claim: The classification accuracy of odorant identity across a 10-fold change in odorant concentration was similar between the concentration-invariant subpopulation of neurons and the entire population of 'generic' neurons.
source: We found that the classification accuracy of odorant identity across a 10-fold change in odorant concentration was similar between the concentration-invariant subpopulation of neurons and the entire population of 'generic' neurons.
evidence: This is based on generalization learning analysis.

claim: For the more difficult generalization tasks across a 100-fold change in odorant concentration, subnetworks of concentration-invariant neurons were much more accurate in predicting odorant identity than the entire population of 'generic' neurons (1% to 0.01% generalization: concentration-invariant cells mean = 63.5 ± 27.1%, Mann-Whitney test n = 13 U=20, Benjamini and Hochberg's FDR adjusted p<0.01, 'generic' neurons mean = 19.2%±17.8%, Mann-Whitney test n = 13 U=82, FDR adjusted p=0.39).
source: However, for the more difficult generalization tasks across a 100-fold change in odorant concentration (0.01% to 1%, and 1% to 0.01%, Figure 5f, red squared boxes), subnetworks of concentration-invariant neurons were much more accurate in predicting odorant identity than the entire population of 'generic' neurons (1% to 0.01% generalization: concentration-invariant cells mean = 63.5 ± 27.1%, Mann-Whitney test n = 13 U=20, Benjamini and Hochberg's FDR adjusted p<0.01, 'generic' neurons mean = 19.2%±17.8%, Mann-Whitney test n = 13 U=82, FDR adjusted p=0.39).
evidence: This demonstrates the superior performance of concentration-invariant neurons in generalization.

claim: For a given set of odorants and concentrations it is possible to identify a subpopulation of piriform neurons that can encode the identity of an odor largely independent of odor intensity.
source: Taken together, these analyses demonstrate that for a given set of odorants and concentrations it is possible to identify a subpopulation of piriform neurons that can encode the identity of an odor largely independent of odor intensity.
evidence: This is a summary of the concentration-invariant neuron findings.

claim: Identifying concentration-invariant neurons across a 10-fold instead of a 100-fold range in odorant concentration yielded 19.2% (±7.4% SD across experiments) concentration-invariant neurons.
source: Using the same selection criteria as for the original data set, this analysis yielded 19.2% (±7.4% SD across experiments) concentration-invariant neurons.
evidence: This tests the stability of concentration-invariant neurons with varying concentration range.

claim: 22% (±8%) of the cells were concentration-invariant for at least one pair of odorants.
source: We found that 22% (±8%) of the cells were concentration-invariant for at least one pair of odorants.
evidence: This tests the stability of concentration-invariant neurons with varying stimulus complexity.

claim: Of the cells concentration-invariant for at least one pair of odorants, 49% were identified as concentration-invariant for all three odorants while the response of the other 51% of cells was modulated by the concentration of one of the three odorants.
source: Of those cells, 49% were identified as concentration-invariant for all three odorants while the response of the other 51% of cells was modulated by the concentration of one of the three odorants.
evidence: This describes the overlap between concentration-invariant neurons for different odorant pairs.

claim: Concentration-invariant subnetworks of neurons can be modulated by stimulus complexity and concentration, yet remain relatively stable within the range of the stimulus set.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that concentration-invariant subnetworks of neurons can be modulated by stimulus complexity and concentration, yet remain relatively stable within the range of our stimulus set.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the stability analysis.

claim: Concentration-invariant neurons did not exhibit response profiles that differentiate them from other neurons in terms of response rise time, duration, peak change in fluorescence, or trial-to-trial variability.
source: We compared response rise time (from 10% to 90% of peak ΔF/F, concentration-invariant neurons: 0.55 ± 0.05 s; generic neurons: 0.52 ± 0.10 s) and duration (width at 50% peak ΔF/F, concentration-invariant neurons: 2.02 ± 0.07 s; generic neurons: 2.01 ± 0.11 s), odor-evoked peak change in fluorescence (deconvolved ΔF/F, concentration-invariant neurons: 10.0 ± 0.7%; generic neurons: 9.2 ± 1.3%), and trial-to-trial variability, but found no significance between the two populations (p>0.05, Wilcoxon ranked sum test, n = 13) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of response properties between concentration-invariant and generic neurons.

claim: Visual inspection of the localization of concentration-invariant cells at individual imaging sites did not reveal obvious clustering.
source: Visual inspection of the localization of concentration-invariant cells at individual imaging sites did not reveal obvious clustering (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of spatial distributions.

claim: The organization of concentration-invariant neurons at 11 out of 13 imaging sites was undistinguishable from the random distribution obtained for shuffled data.
source: Furthermore, performing the statistical analysis based on the nearest neighbor index (see Figure 3), we found that the organization of concentration-invariant neurons at 11 out of 13 imaging sites was undistinguishable from the random distribution obtained for shuffled data.
evidence: This is based on nearest neighbor index analysis.

claim: In 2 of the 13 imaging sites, spatial distributions of concentration-invariant neurons were moderately but significantly different from random.
source: In 2 of the 13 imaging sites, spatial distributions were moderately but significantly different from random.
evidence: This is based on nearest neighbor index analysis.

claim: A subpopulation of piriform neurons, with response profiles and spatial distributions that are similar to other odor-responsive neurons, encode odor identity independent of concentration.
source: Taken together, our analysis identifies a subpopulation of piriform neurons, with response profiles and spatial distributions that are similar to other odor-responsive neurons, but which encode odor identity independent of concentration.
evidence: This is a summary of the concentration-invariant neuron characterization.

claim: Considerable normalization of odor-evoked neural activity across a range of odorant concentrations has been observed in the olfactory bulb.
source: Considerable normalization of odor-evoked neural activity across a range of odorant concentrations has been observed in the olfactory bulb (Banerjee et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2013; Miyamichi et al., 2013; Roland et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2013), suggesting that concentration-invariant piriform odor responses could be inherited from the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This summarizes prior findings from the literature.

claim: The formation of segregated, concentration-invariant odor identity representations in subpopulations of piriform neurons may emerge within cortex itself.
source: Alternatively, the formation of segregated, concentration-invariant odor identity representations in subpopulations of piriform neurons may emerge within cortex itself.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis to be tested.

claim: 25.9% ± 14.9% of mitral and tufted cells exhibited odorant-selective responses.
source: Consistent with this impression, our analysis of variance indicated that 25.9% ± 14.9% of neurons exhibited odorant-selective responses.
evidence: This is based on ANOVA analysis of mitral and tufted cell responses.

claim: Of the odorant-selective mitral and tufted cells, only 20.5 ± 15.1%, constituting only 5.2 ± 5.9% of the total population were concentration-invariant.
source: Of these, only 20.5 ± 15.1%, constituting only 5.2 ± 5.9% of the total population were concentration-invariant.
evidence: This is based on ANOVA analysis of mitral and tufted cell responses.

claim: Many fewer neurons were exclusively modulated by odorant identity in the olfactory bulb compared to the piriform cortex (olfactory bulb, 5.2 ± 5.9%, piriform cortex 10.4 ± 4.5%, Mann-Whitney test, nob = 19, npir = 13, U = 59, p<0.01).
source: Thus, many fewer neurons were exclusively modulated by odorant identity in the olfactory bulb compared to the piriform cortex (Figure 7d) (olfactory bulb, 5.2 ± 5.9%, piriform cortex 10.4 ± 4.5%, Mann-Whitney test, nob = 19, npir = 13, U = 59, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between olfactory bulb and piriform cortex.

claim: The fraction of concentration-invariant cells in piriform cortex is consistently and significantly higher than that observed in the olfactory bulb, independent of sampling size and the significance criterion used.
source: We find that the fraction of concentration-invariant cells in piriform cortex is consistently and significantly higher than that observed in the olfactory bulb, independent of sampling size and the significance criterion used in our model (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on subsampling and sensitivity analysis.

claim: Shuffling mitral cell identities across stimuli resulted in the identification of the same percentage of concentration-invariant neurons observed experimentally (bootstrap mean 3.9 ± 0.8%; observed value 5.5%, p=0.073).
source: Shuffling mitral cell identities across stimuli indeed resulted in the identification of the same percentage of concentration-invariant neurons observed experimentally (bootstrap mean 3.9 ± 0.8%; observed value 5.5%, p=0.073).
evidence: This is based on bootstrap analysis.

claim: Shuffling cell identities from the piriform dataset yielded significantly fewer concentration-invariant neurons than observed experimentally (bootstrap mean 5.3 ± 0.41%; observed value 11.7%, p<0.001).
source: By contrast, shuffling cell identities from the piriform dataset yielded significantly fewer concentration-invariant neurons than observed experimentally (bootstrap mean 5.3 ± 0.41%; observed value 11.7%, p<0.001, Figure 7e).
evidence: This is based on bootstrap analysis.

claim: The observed number of concentration-invariant neurons in piriform was above chance in 8 out of 13 imaging sites.
source: We found that the observed number of concentration-invariant neurons in piriform was above chance in 8 out of 13 imaging sites.
evidence: This is based on bootstrap analysis at individual imaging sites.

claim: Only 2 out of 19 mitral and tufted cell imaging sites contained concentration-invariant neurons above chance level.
source: In contrast, only 2 out of 19 mitral and tufted cell imaging sites contained concentration-invariant neurons above chance level (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is based on bootstrap analysis at individual imaging sites.

claim: The encoding of odor identity independent of concentration is robust in piriform cortex, but not in olfactory bulb mitral and tufted cells.
source: Together, these results indicate that the encoding of odor identity independent of concentration is robust in piriform cortex, but not in olfactory bulb mitral and tufted cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparison between piriform cortex and olfactory bulb.

claim: Despite substantial overlap between response patterns evoked by different odorants, odor identity could correctly be predicted from local ensembles of piriform neurons.
source: We found that despite substantial overlap between response patterns evoked by different odorants, odor identity could correctly be predicted from local ensembles of piriform neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Piriform response patterns across the population change substantially with increasing odorant concentration, potentially confounding odor identification.
source: Furthermore, we observed that piriform response patterns across the population change substantially with increasing odorant concentration, potentially confounding odor identification.
evidence: This is a summary of the concentration-dependent changes.

claim: A substantial fraction of odor-selective piriform neurons exhibit largely concentration-invariant odor responses.
source: However, a substantial fraction of odor-selective piriform neurons exhibit largely concentration-invariant odor responses, and odor identity - independent of intensity - could accurately be decoded from this subpopulation of piriform neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the concentration-invariant neuron findings.

claim: Concentration-invariant neurons are overrepresented in piriform cortex but not in olfactory bulb mitral and tufted cells.
source: Concentration-invariant neurons are overrepresented in piriform cortex but not in olfactory bulb mitral and tufted cells, suggesting that concentration-invariant subnetworks for odor identity emerge in cortical neural circuits for olfaction.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparison between piriform cortex and olfactory bulb.

claim: Concentration-invariant subnetworks for odor identity emerge in cortical neural circuits for olfaction.
source: Concentration-invariant neurons are overrepresented in piriform cortex but not in olfactory bulb mitral and tufted cells, suggesting that concentration-invariant subnetworks for odor identity emerge in cortical neural circuits for olfaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparison between piriform cortex and olfactory bulb.

claim: Previous immunohistochemical, electrophysiological and imaging experiments have revealed that piriform odor representations are distributed across a large area of the cortex, and that piriform neurons display discontinuous receptive fields.
source: Previous immunohistochemical, electrophysiological and imaging experiments have revealed that piriform odor representations are distributed across a large area of the cortex, and that piriform neurons display discontinuous receptive fields (Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Rennaker et al., 2007; Stettler and Axel, 2009; Yoshida and Mori, 2007).
evidence: This summarizes prior findings from the literature.

claim: These observations led to the speculation that information about odor is encoded by ensembles of coordinately active neurons distributed across piriform cortex without topographic organization.
source: These observations led to the speculation that information about odor is encoded by ensembles of coordinately active neurons distributed across piriform cortex without topographic organization (Stettler and Axel, 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work.

claim: Odor identity could indeed be decoded from spatially distributed patterns of odor-evoked piriform activity.
source: Here, we explicitly tested this prediction, and we found that odor identity could indeed be decoded from spatially distributed patterns of odor-evoked piriform activity.
evidence: This confirms the hypothesis from prior work.

claim: The results are consistent with recent data from extracellular recordings in awake rats and mice, which show that odor identity can be accurately decoded from the firing rates of piriform neural ensembles.
source: Our results are consistent with recent data from extracellular recordings in awake rats (Miura et al., 2012) and mice (see co-submitted manuscript by Bolding and Franks), which show that odor identity can be accurately decoded from the firing rates of piriform neural ensembles.
evidence: This relates the current findings to other studies.

claim: Extracellular recordings cannot reveal the spatial organization of the neurons that participate in odor coding.
source: However, extracellular recordings cannot reveal the spatial organization of the neurons that participate in odor coding.
evidence: This is a limitation of extracellular recordings.

claim: The results provide robust evidence that odor information is encoded without topographic organization by ensembles of piriform neurons.
source: Thus, our results provide robust evidence that odor information is encoded without topographic organization by ensembles of piriform neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the spatial analysis.

claim: The majority of piriform neurons are narrowly tuned to odor, exhibit high trial-to-trial variability to repeated presentations of the same odor, and substantial overlap between response patterns elicited by different odors.
